summary.title: What Do You Visualize While Programming?
summary.one_liner: Programmers form mental images while problem solving, and the most useful visualization (boxes-and-arrows diagrams, ER diagrams, traces, treemaps, call-tree views) depends on the task.
takeaways: Programming happens inside the head, so the mental images a programmer uses shape how well they solve problems.
Match the visualization to the task: boxes-and-arrows for systems design, ER diagrams for schemas, traces and flamegraphs for optimization, treemaps for space usage.
For algorithms, step through data state line by line; for recursion, track the call stack or use a tree representation, starting with base cases.
Externalize complex images onto paper or screen when they exceed working memory, then iterate on the next step.
Improve by researching available tools and diagrams and adopting the one that best fits a problem.
summary.summary: The author opens with Richard Feynman's counting example to argue that people store and picture the same concepts differently, and briefly mentions aphantasia. He then walks through task-specific visualizations: systems design diagrams, database ER diagrams (DBeaver mentioned), traces and flamegraphs for optimization, treemaps for memory or disk, step-by-step data views for algorithms, and call-stack or tree views for recursion. The post ends with advice for beginners and advanced programmers to refine their mental models, plus a reading list of related essays on software visualization.
